title: The Effectiveness of Explanatory Adaptive Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether explanatory adaptive feedback in a digital educational game improves students’ fraction learning beyond corrective feedback alone. The study is motivated by persistent difficulties children have with fraction magnitude understanding, including misconceptions such as natural number bias and unit-of-reference errors, as well as the role of non-cognitive factors like math anxiety, motivation, and self-concept.

The intervention used the Number Trace Fraction game, a number-line estimation learning environment. Students received one of three conditions: a game with corrective feedback, the same game with explanatory adaptive feedback tailored to likely misconceptions, or an active control condition using non-fraction math learning tracks. The adaptive version changed textual and visual feedback based on students’ estimation accuracy and included additional scaffolds such as simplification notation and animated agents. The study was conducted with fourth graders in regular classrooms in Flanders, Belgium, over six training sessions spanning roughly 3–4 weeks, with pretest, posttest, and two-month retention testing.

Results showed that both experimental conditions improved near transfer fraction knowledge relative to the control group, but explanatory adaptive feedback did not outperform corrective feedback. Far transfer fraction knowledge improved over time across conditions, suggesting some influence of regular curriculum exposure rather than the game alone. For non-cognitive outcomes, explanatory adaptive feedback was associated with a reduction in trait math anxiety without the motivational decline seen in some other conditions, but it did not improve math self-concept. The authors conclude that adaptive feedback may have promise, but the current implementation was not fine-grained enough to yield cognitive benefits beyond corrective feedback.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a well-designed randomized intervention study with an active control group, pre/post/retention testing, and multilevel modeling. Credibility is strong, but some concerns remain about weak internal consistency for the fraction measures and limited evidence that the adaptive component was actually processed.
impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear positive effects for near transfer compared with control, but the added adaptive feedback produced no measurable gain over corrective feedback and effect sizes for the main comparative claim are not reported. Overall impact is therefore modest and somewhat unclear beyond the base game intervention.

interventions.use_case: digital educational game for fraction number line estimation with adaptive feedback and scaffolds to address misconceptions (natural number bias, unit of reference) in fourth graders
rule-based corrective versus explanatory adaptive feedback on fraction number line estimation tasks, including misconception-specific text, visual highlights, and scaffolding agents
system-adapted feedback delivered based on students' response accuracy during gameplay, with predefined thresholds and feedback areas

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized study of 288 fourth graders, near transfer fraction knowledge improved significantly from pretest to posttest and retention in both experimental game conditions, but not in the active control condition. However, explanatory adaptive feedback did not outperform corrective feedback alone on fraction knowledge; far transfer also showed only time effects, with gains from pre- to posttest for corrective feedback and from pre- to retention for all conditions.
finding.measure: Near transfer fraction knowledge (10-item number line estimation test) and far transfer fraction knowledge (10-item procedural/conceptual fraction test)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention had mixed effects on motivational and emotional outcomes. Trait math motivation decreased in the control condition and corrective feedback condition, while trait math anxiety decreased only in the explanatory adaptive feedback condition; state math motivation also decreased over time in the corrective condition, but no significant state anxiety effects were found.
finding.measure: Trait math motivation, trait math anxiety, state math motivation, state math anxiety, state math self-concept

finding.finding_summary: State math self-concept was significantly lower in both experimental game conditions than in the active control condition across five training sessions, suggesting the fraction game was experienced as challenging. The paper reports a significant condition effect for state self-concept but does not provide a standardized effect size in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: State math self-concept collected after each training session
